item.title: UNICEF welcomes the release of women and children in Kenscoff and calls for stronger protection of children in Haiti
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: UN Children's Fund

PORT-AU-PRINCE, 28 August 2026 - Six children and seven women who were abducted in Kenscoff last Sunday have been released. The children include three children under the age of two, a seven-year-old and two teenage girls. UNICEF and community leaders supported efforts that contributed to their release, ending days of captivity.

“This release offers a rare moment of hope amid the violence threatening children in Haiti,” said UNICEF Deputy Representative in Haiti, Yannig Dussart. “The Kenscoff abduction was not an isolated incident but another stark reminder of the scale and frequency of attacks on children across the country.”

Armed violence continues to grip Haiti, placing children in continued danger. Killings, abductions and other grave violations have become a consistent threat to children.

UNICEF continues to work with all key stakeholders to strengthen child protection systems, support children affected by violence, and enable their recovery and reintegration. UNICEF calls on all armed actors in Haiti to cease attacks on children and release any children still held immediately and ensure their protection at all times.
item.author: UN Children's Fund

item.title: L’UNICEF salue la liberation des enfants et des femmes enlevés à Kenscoff et appelle à renforcer la protection des enfants en Haiti
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: UN Children's Fund

PORT-AU-PRINCE, 28 août 2026 – Six enfants et sept femmes enlevés dimanche dernier à Kenscoff ont été libérés. Parmi les enfants figurent trois enfants âgés de moins de 2 ans, un enfant de 7 ans et deux adolescentes. L’UNICEF et des responsables communautaires ont soutenu les efforts ayant contribué à leur libération, mettant ainsi fin à plusieurs jours de captivité.

« Cette libération offre un rare moment d’espoir face à la violence qui menace les enfants en Haïti », a déclaré Yannig Dussart, Représentant adjoint de l’UNICEF en Haïti. « L’enlèvement de Kenscoff n’était pas un incident isolé, mais un nouveau rappel brutal de l’ampleur et de la fréquence des attaques contre les enfants à travers le pays. »

La violence armée continue de frapper Haïti, exposant les enfants à des dangers persistants. Les meurtres, les enlèvements et d’autres violations graves constituent désormais une menace constante pour les enfants.

L’UNICEF continue de travailler avec l’ensemble des acteurs clés afin de renforcer les systèmes de protection de l’enfance, de soutenir les enfants touchés par la violence et d’accompagner leur rétablissement et leur réintégration.

L’UNICEF appelle tous les acteurs armés en Haïti à mettre fin aux attaques contre les enfants, à libérer immédiatement tout enfant encore détenu et à garantir leur protection en toutes circonstances.

item.title: Remarks to the Security Council by the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs

Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH) Carlos Ruiz Massieu

Remarks to the Security Council on Haiti

Port-au-Prince, 26 August 2026

[as delivered]

Madam President,

Distinguished Members of the Security Council,

Thank you very much for convening this urgent meeting of the Security Council on Haiti. I address you today in the aftermath of another appalling atrocity inflicted upon the Haitian population.

As this Council is aware, during the night of 23 to 24 August, gangs launched a brutal attack against the commune of Kenscoff, in the hills overlooking Port-au-Prince.

This assault claimed the lives of at least 47 persons, including three boys and two girls, left dozens abducted and many others injured, and caused further displacement and suffering.

Homes were also set ablaze, and local population seeking refuge from the violence was attacked, including at a church, where gang members executed people in a courtyard and killed others as they attempted to escape.

It is with profound grief and sadness that I join the Secretary-General in condemning these horrific acts in the strongest possible terms.

And I call for the immediate and unconditional release of all persons that were abducted, including women and children.

Madam President,

This massacre is deeply shocking, but it is not an isolated tragedy.

It is the latest in a series of attacks affecting the commune of Kenscoff since early 2025 and demonstrates the continued capacity and determination of gangs to terrorize the population, expand their influence beyond the capital and pose a direct challenge to state authority. Haitians continue to pay a devastating and intolerable human cost, with BINUH documenting more than 1,400 people killed and more than 600 injured between April and June 2026 alone.

The attack in Kenscoff has generated a new wave of public indignation across all sectors of Haiti’s society, as well as international partners, with renewed calls to protect populations, strengthen security institutions and restore public order. These reactions reflect a growing recognition that security is the foundation for progress in all other areas.

Madam President,

Distinguished members,

This latest heartbreaking episode is a stark reminder of the urgent need to further strengthen international security support for Haiti.

In this regard, I welcome the decision by the national authorities on 26 August to bring together the Haitian National Police, the Armed Forces and the GSF – the Gang Suppression Force – to jointly assess these latest developments and coordinate operational plans and deployments on the ground. Notably, it was agreed that the Gang Suppression Force would strengthen its presence in the Port-au-Prince area, while the national security forces would reinforce with additional elements their deployment in Kenscoff.

National security institutions cannot be left to confront this threat without adequate support. The GSF represents clearly a critical component of the international response authorized by this Council. Its swift and full deployment is of the essence.

Sustained cooperation and coordination among national authorities and with the GSF will remain essential to address insecurity, protect communities and restore confidence among Haitians.

For far too long, Haitians have lived in fear of being killed, kidnapped or subjected to sexual violence.

Madam President,

This latest attack occurs at a critical moment in Haiti’s political transition.

Without improved security conditions, efforts to strengthen governance, accelerate the political process and advance electoral preparations will remain severely constrained and vulnerable to setbacks.

At the same time, as I emphasized before this Council in last July, and as the events in Kenscoff have tragically demonstrated, security operations will not be sufficient to produce sustainable security gains.

These security efforts must be accompanied by measures to restore State authority, basic services, and economic and social activity in affected communities.

This requires a coherent approach linking security operations to stabilization and recovery, community violence reduction, the reopening of schools and health facilities, and livelihood opportunities.

It also requires credible pathways for disengagement from gangs, particularly for children and young people recruited and exploited by gangs.

Madam President,

Distinguished Members of the Council,

Equally important is breaking the cycle of impunity.

The perpetrators of the attack of Kenscoff, as well as those who finance, arm and enable gang violence must brought to acount.

The effective activation and operationalization of the specialized judicial units mandated to investigate mass crimes, sexual violence, financial crimes --including the prompt opening of investigations into the Kenscoff’s attack -- will be paramount to strengthen the rule of law and restore public confidence in State institutions.

Madam President,

Expressions of concern are important and reflect our solidarity with the Haitian people, but they must be accompanied by sustained action. Haiti urgently needs existing commitments to translate into concrete results.

The UN, the United Nations as a whole, remains fully committed to supporting Haitian-led efforts to improve security, advance the political process and create the conditions necessary for a peaceful, inclusive and stable country.

I thank you, madame President.

item.title: Haiti: Haïti | SMART 2026 – Fiche d'information sur les résultats préliminaires (Publication: août 2026)
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Sources: Government of Haiti, Nutrition Cluster, UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

CONTEXTE

La situation nutritionnelle chez les enfants de moins de 5 ans et chez les femmes âgées de 15 à 49 ans en Haïti demeure précaire et résulte d'une combinaison de facteurs structurels et conjoncturels. Les crises sécuritaire, économique et humanitaire qui affectent le pays depuis plusieurs années ont fortement dégradé l'accès des ménages à une alimentation adéquate, aux services de santé essentiels et aux interventions de nutrition. Les dernières analyses IPC font état de niveaux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire aiguë, susceptibles d’accroître davantage le risque de malnutrition chez les personnes les plus vulnérables.

Compte tenu du contexte actuel et afin de disposer d’informations fiables et actualisées sur les indicateurs nutritionnels, une nouvelle enquête nationale a été réalisée trois ans après celle de 2023. L’enquête nutritionnelle nationale SMART 2026 L'enquête a débuté le 9 mai avec la formation des référents, suivi de la formation des enquêteurs et enfin la collecte des données du 1er au 16 juillet 2026 et visait à évaluer l’état nutritionnel des enfants âgés de 0 à 59 mois et des femmes âgées de 15 à 49 ans, ainsi qu’à estimer la mortalité rétrospective dans la population générale et chez les enfants de moins de 5 ans à l’échelle nationale.

item.title: Mr. Indrika Ratwatte, Acting ASG for Humanitarian Affairs, on behalf of Mr. Tom Fletcher, USG for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator – Briefing to the Security Council on Haiti, 28 August 2026
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

New York, 28 August 2026

As delivered

Madam President, Excellencies,

Building on the political and security developments outlined by the SRSG [Special Representative of the Secretary-General] Ruiz Massieu, allow me to focus on the rapidly worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti – one of the most severe in the Western Hemisphere.

Families are fleeing violence. Hunger is rising. Health services are crumbling.

More than half of Haiti’s population – some 6.4 million people – are in need of humanitarian assistance.

The latest attack on Kenscoff is yet another grim reminder, as the SRSG mentioned, of the suffering Haitians face every day: Dozens of people were killed, and more than 2,600 forced to flee their homes, many for the second or third time. Over 50 people were reportedly abducted. Families are still searching for missing relatives, while communities face widespread trauma, displacement and uncertainty about the fate of their loved ones.

And violence is not the only threat.

Haiti remains highly vulnerable to recurring climate shocks and other natural hazards. Hurricane Melissa brought death and destruction to Haiti last year, and now the country is facing another hurricane season. And recent seismic activity in the region is a stark reminder of Haiti’s vulnerability to earthquakes.

Madam President,

Nearly 1.5 million people – 12 per cent of Haiti’s population – are internally displaced. Half of them are children.

Displacement doubled in just two years and conditions in many displacement sites are squalid. Sites are overcrowded and unsafe, without adequate water and sanitation facilities.

Even as more people are displaced in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and Artibonite department, families are returning home in parts of the West and Centre departments – including to areas where conditions for safe, voluntary and sustainable returns have not yet been established.

People must be able to return home safely and voluntarily.

Meanwhile, deportations to Haiti continue at scale. In the first eight months of 2026, we have seen almost 200,000 people were forcibly returned, a 10 per cent increase compared with the same period last year.

Many arrive without resources, documentation or support networks, and some have especially urgent protection needs, including survivors of sexual violence, pregnant and lactating women, people with disabilities, and unaccompanied and separated children.

Madam President,

Shocking levels of violence and suffering are inflicted on the population – particularly on women, girls and children.

Our humanitarian partners have recorded over 5,500 incidents of gender-based violence, or about 30 cases each day, in the first six months of the year alone.

Women and girls constitute the vast majority of survivors. Approximately 70 per cent of reported incidents of gender-based violence involved rape, and nearly three quarters of reported rape cases involved collective rape.

Women and girls are being subjected to horrific sexual violence with utter impunity. This must stop.

The trauma of survivors is visible on their faces, while access to timely and comprehensive services remains extremely limited.

Protecting women and girls from gender-based violence is a collective responsibility.

Madam President,

For Haiti’s children, life is a daily struggle for survival.

Half of all displaced people are children, with more than 2.6 million children across the country in need of humanitarian assistance.

Hospitals are overwhelmed, with childhoods cut short by violence, neglect, exploitation and hunger.

According to UNICEF, the number of children recruited and used by armed groups skyrocketed by an estimated 200 per cent in 2025.

The connection is clear. When children go hungry, lose access to school or are separated from their families, they become more vulnerable to recruitment. In some areas, these groups are seen as one of the few sources of food, income, shelter or protection.

Once recruited, getting out can be extraordinarily difficult. Children face threats of retaliation, few safe alternatives, and stigma within their families and communities. They also become a target of more violence.

Education is one of the strongest protections.

Yet as the school year starts, attacks on and the use of schools by armed groups continue to disrupt learning.

More than 1,600 schools remain closed, affecting 7,500 teachers and depriving more than 240,000 students of learning.

Every day out of school leaves children more exposed to violence, exploitation and recruitment.

The children of Haiti deserve a future, not more violence.

Madam President,

The crisis is also depriving people of reaching essential services.

Healthcare, livelihoods, water and sanitation continue to be disrupted by violence and insecurity. Just 10 per cent of health facilities with inpatient capacity remain operational in Port-au-Prince, including only one public hospital.

Attacks on healthcare, including ambulances, and movement restrictions continue to limit access to life-saving services.

Madam President,

We must also protect the humanitarian space that allows us to reach people in need.

As we do in other crises, the UN and our partners operate on the basis of humanitarian principles in all areas of need – irrespective of who controls or influences them – to ensure that life-saving aid can reach vulnerable people wherever they are.

Humanitarians must not be criminalized for engaging with armed groups when necessary to reach people in need, or for providing life-saving medical care to people injured during security operations.

There must be a clear and visible distinction between humanitarian and security actors to ensure the safety of aid workers and preserve access to – and the trust of – communities.

At the same time, the ongoing dialogue between humanitarians and security actors, including the Gang Suppression Force, through the Civil Military Coordination Cell chaired by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, is a critical element, and we appreciate the close cooperation that exists.

Madam President,

Behind the figures I outlined are families repeatedly uprooted, children separated from parents, and communities stripped of even the most basic services.

Humanitarians are staying and delivering.

Together, our humanitarian partners reached more than 2.4 million people during the first half of this year.

But many of the most acute needs are in areas where access depends on sustained engagement – with security forces, armed groups, and others – and on the long-term acceptance of humanitarian action by communities.

That trust remains fragile. Preserving it requires strict adherence to humanitarian principles –particularly neutrality, impartiality and independence – and a clear distinction between humanitarian actors and political or security actors.

And emergency aid alone cannot change the trajectory of this crisis.

Let me close with three asks:

First, stop the violence. No child should fall asleep to gunfire. Hospitals, schools and aid workers must never be targets.

Second, fund the response. Humanitarian organizations remain committed and ready to deliver life‑saving assistance, but surging needs mean we need continued predictable and flexible funding. We thank our largest donors – the United States, the European Commission, the World Bank and Canada – for their support.

And third, tackle the causes of this crisis. Lasting progress requires broader efforts – including in the realms of security, political stability, and sustained investment in essential services.

The people of Haiti deserve more than mere survival.

They deserve safety, opportunity, and hope for a better future.

Thank you.

item.title: Nearly one in thirteen children under five suffer from acute malnutrition in Haiti
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: UN Children's Fund

New national nutrition survey shows acute malnutrition among children has increased since 2023

PORT-AU-PRINCE/NEW YORK, 28 August 2026 – Approximately one in thirteen children in Haiti aged between 6 months and 5 years old are suffering from acute malnutrition, according to the preliminary findings by the 2026 National Nutrition SMART Survey released today.

The prevalence of global acute malnutrition in children in Haiti aged 6 to 59 months, defined as moderate or severe wasting or nutritional swelling, has increased from 5.1 per cent to 7.4 per cent from 2023 to 2026.

“The findings emerge against a backdrop of prolonged insecurity, economic hardship and humanitarian needs that continue to constrain families’ access to sufficient nutritious food, health care and nutrition services,” said UNICEF Deputy Representative in Haiti, Yannig Dussart. “Preventing and treating malnutrition in Haiti requires urgent action and attention by stakeholders and actors to ensure children can access the lifesaving services they need.”

Acute malnutrition, which occurs when children do not receive enough nutritious food or suffer from repeated illness, can rapidly become life-threatening without timely treatment. Children affected by severe acute malnutrition are at high risk of death, particularly when combined with illness and limited access to medical care.

Between 2023 and 2025, grave violations against children, which include denial of access to humanitarian support and attacks on schools and hospitals where children receive nutritional services, have tripled.

Despite these worsening trends in acute malnutrition, the survey shows progress in other indicators. The prevalence of chronic malnutrition, or stunting, among children under five declined from 22.8 per cent in 2023 to 17.3 per cent in 2026. Early initiation of breastfeeding increased from 48 per cent in 2023 to 68.0 per cent in 2026, while exclusive breastfeeding rose from 17.5 per cent to 33.0 per cent.

UNICEF and its partners are working with the Ministry of Public Health and Population to scale up the screening and treatment of malnourished children, including through community health workers and mobile teams operating in hard-to-reach and insecure areas. A fuller analysis of the survey results, combined with an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification for Acute Malnutrition (IPC-AMN), is expected in the coming month and will guide the humanitarian and development response.

As humanitarian needs continue to worsen in Haiti, UNICEF is urgently calling for increased support to address a funding gap of more than 64 per cent for nutrition interventions under its 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal. Sustained investment is critical to prevent, detect, and treat acute malnutrition, maintain the supply of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF), and expand access to essential nutrition services for vulnerable children and women. With adequate resources, UNICEF and its partners can save lives, protect children from the devastating consequences of malnutrition, and ensure that those most at risk receive the care and support they urgently need.

#####

Note to editors:

The SMART Survey 2026 provides a population-based assessment of the nutritional status of children aged 0–59 months and women aged 15–49 years living within areas of Haiti in July 2026. The survey assessed important factors related to child and maternal nutrition, including childhood illness, infant and young child feeding practices, measles and rubella vaccination coverage, vitamin A supplementation, deworming and care-seeking behavior.

The SMART survey is a standardized methodology for measuring nutritional status, providing humanitarian agencies with reliable data to guide the response. The findings are specific to the survey period and do not provide information about nutritional conditions before or after the survey period, nor do they serve as a nationally representative statistic for international comparison

This national survey was conducted by the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP), through the Coordination Unit of the National Food and Nutrition Programme (UCPNaNu), with technical and financial support from UNICEF, made possible by the support of the Governments of the United States and of Canada and of German Committee for UNICEF.

item.title: Haiti: Haití: Urgen justicia y protección tras ataque mortal de bandas armadas en Kenscoff
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: Amnesty International

Amnistía Internacional condena la matanza ocurrida durante la noche del 23 al 24 de agosto en Kenscoff, cerca de Puerto Príncipe. Al menos 47 personas murieron y 22 resultaron heridas, según Naciones Unidas, mientras que decenas de personas habrían sido secuestradas. Entre las personas atacadas se encontrarían personas desplazadas por la violencia que se refugiaban en una iglesia.

“Lamentablemente, volvemos a ver una nueva masacre en Haití. Esto es un recordatorio del devastador costo humano derivado de la ausencia de políticas efectivas de protección de la población. Instamos a las autoridades haitianas y a la comunidad internacional a redoblar sus esfuerzos para proteger a la población frente a la escalada de violencia de las bandas armadas. Las personas sospechosas de responsabilidad penal por estos asesinatos, secuestros y otros graves abusos contra los derechos humanos deben ser identificadas y llevadas ante la justicia en juicios justos”, dijo Astrid Valencia, directora adjunta de Investigación para las Américas de Amnistía Internacional.

«Los refuerzos y las operaciones de seguridad anunciados por el gobierno deben tener como prioridad la protección de la población y de las personas secuestradas y llevarse a cabo con pleno respeto de los derechos humanos”,reafirmó Astrid Valencia, directora adjunta de Investigación para las Américas de Amnistía Internacional

“El secuestro de personas y las amenazas contra sus vidas agravan aún más una situación ya estremecedora. Las bandas armadas deben liberar inmediatamente y sin condiciones a todas las personas secuestradas y poner fin a los asesinatos, secuestros y demás ataques contra la población. Las autoridades haitianas deben adoptar todas las medidas a su alcance, respetando plenamente los derechos humanos, para proteger la vida y la integridad de las personas retenidas.

La población haitiana tiene derecho a vivir sin el temor constante de ser asesinada, secuestrada o forzada a abandonar sus hogares. Como hemos advertido reiteradamente tras otras matanzas como las ocurridas en Cité Soleil, Labodri y Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite, seguirá existiendo un grave riesgo de nuevas pérdidas de vidas mientras no se adopten medidas urgentes y sostenibles para proteger a las comunidades y romper el ciclo de violencia e impunidad. La comunidad internacional debe apoyar de manera urgente y sostenida a las autoridades haitianas para que cumplan con su obligación de proteger a la población y garantizar justicia por estos crímenes”, concluyo Astrid Valencia.

Para más información o para concertar una entrevista, por favor contacte a press@amnesty.org

item.title: Haiti: Justice and protection urgently needed following deadly armed gang attack in Kenscoff
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: Amnesty International

Amnesty International condemns the massacre that took place during the night of 23–24 August in Kenscoff, near Port-au-Prince. At least 47 people were killed and 22 injured, according to the United Nations, while dozens of people were reportedly abducted. Those attacked reportedly included people displaced by violence who had sought refuge in a church.

“Sadly, we are once again witnessing another massacre in Haiti. This is a reminder of the devastating human cost of the absence of effective policies to protect the population. We urge the Haitian authorities and the international community to redouble their efforts to protect people from the escalating violence by armed gangs. Anyone suspected of criminal responsibility for these killings, abductions and other serious human rights abuses must be identified and brought to justice in fair trials,” said Astrid Valencia, Deputy Regional Director for Research for the Americas at Amnesty International.

Sadly, we are once again witnessing another massacre in Haiti. This is a reminder of the devastating human cost of the absence of effective policies to protect the population.”

Astrid Valencia, Deputy Regional Director for Research for the Americas at Amnesty International.

“The reinforcements and security operations announced by the government must prioritize the protection of the population and of those who have been abducted, and must be carried out in full compliance with human rights,” reiterated Astrid Valencia, Deputy Regional Director for Research for the Americas at Amnesty International.

The reinforcements and security operations announced by the government must prioritize the protection of the population and of those who have been abducted, and must be carried out in full compliance with human rights.”

Astrid Valencia, Deputy Regional Director for Research for the Americas at Amnesty International.

“The abduction of people and threats to their lives further aggravate an already horrifying situation. Armed gangs must immediately and unconditionally release all those they have abducted and put an end to killings, abductions and other attacks against the population. The Haitian authorities must take all measures within their power, in full compliance with human rights, to protect the lives and physical integrity of those being held.

“The Haitian population has the right to live without the constant fear of being killed, abducted or forced to flee their homes. As we have repeatedly warned following other massacres, including those in Cité Soleil, Labodri and Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite, there will continue to be a serious risk of further loss of life unless urgent and sustainable measures are taken to protect communities and break the cycle of violence and impunity. The international community must provide urgent and sustained support to the Haitian authorities so that they can fulfil their obligation to protect the population and ensure justice for these crimes,” concluded Astrid Valencia.

For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact press@amnesty.org

item.title: Quarterly report on the Human Rights Situation in Haiti, April - June 2026
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: UN Integrated Office in Haiti

Please refer to the attached file.

  • 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured: 55% by gangs, 5% by self-defense groups and members of the population, and 40% during security forces’ operations against gangs.
  • Expansion of gang attacks in the Artibonite department and incursions by the Village de Dieu gang into the South-East department.
  • Increase in kidnappings between April and June, with 51 victims in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area. At least 796 victims of gang-related sexual violence were recorded.
  • At least 9 members of the population killed or injured by explosive drones, including 6 children.
  • Significant decrease in extrajudicial executions and attempted executions (14 cases) committed by police officers, compared with 2025.
  • 3 police officers were killed and 2 others injured.
  • Inauguration of the premises of the specialized judicial units (pôles judiciaires spécialisés) to combat mass crimes, including sexual violence, and financial crimes, and progress in the assignment of magistrates and staff designated for their operation.

Au cours de la journée du mardi 28 juillet 2026, des membres du GCO de Savien, accompagnés de Kokorat San Ras, ont attaqué la commune de Saint-Michel de l’Attalaye, plus précisément la 7e section communale de Marmont, localité Nan Paul.

D’après les informations recueillies, le groupe était composé de douze (12) individus lourdement armés. Ils ont fait irruption dans la section communale ce mardi 28 juillet, jour de marché. Au cours de l’attaque, ils ont installé un poste de péage illégal et ont procédé à la fouille des personnes se rendant au marché ou en revenant.

À la suite de cette attaque, la population a quitté la section de Marmont pour se réfugier dans des communes et localités voisines : Saint-Michel de l’Attalaye (Platana, Carmathe, L’Hermithe et Centre-Ville), Gonaïves et Ennery.

item.title: Haiti: Women risk their lives to reach sexual and reproductive healthcare in Port-au-Prince
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

In Port-au-Prince, Haiti, every movement poses a risk. For thousands of women, seeing a doctor, obtaining contraceptives, attending prenatal check-ups, or receiving care after sexual assault has become fraught with obstacles.

In a capital where armed violence is undermining an already fragile health system, access to sexual and reproductive healthcare is increasingly limited. Yet such care remains essential at every stage of life.

A collapsing health system

One recent morning, a 29-year-old woman was admitted, barely conscious, to the Isaïe Jeanty Maternity hospital, which is supported by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). She had developed postpartum eclampsia – a serious complication that can be fatal without prompt treatment – after giving birth at home a few hours earlier.

Her stepfather accompanied her on a motorcycle from Cité Soleil, a commune of Port-au-Prince, with her newborn baby in his arms.

“I was shaking when I arrived; I thought it was a lost cause,” he says in the maternity ward, where about 15 women are being monitored by medical teams. “This morning, she looked as if she were dead. But now she's almost smiling. It's as if she had been brought back to life.”

This morning, she looked as if she were dead. But now she's almost smiling. It's as if she had been brought back to life.Stepfather of an MSF patient

Haiti has the highest maternal mortality ratio in the Americas. The World Health Organization estimates that it stood at 328 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2023, compared to 197 globally and 58 in the Americas region.1

These numbers illustrate the gradual collapse of a health system weakened by the expansion of armed groups, institutional instability and chronic underfunding of public services. In Port-au-Prince, many health facilities have closed their doors, thus severely reducing access to essential healthcare — especially for women and their sexual and reproductive healthcare.

Many pregnancies are not monitored by trained professionals, and births take place at home without medical assistance. Without timely access to healthcare, complications, such as eclampsia, haemorrhages, infections, or neonatal distress, may be detected too late.

“We had to refer a woman at eight months of pregnancy to give birth to her baby who died in utero,” says a midwife at an MSF mobile clinic. “She had never been able to receive prenatal check-ups. This should not be happening. These are preventable complications that become fatal without medical support.”

Multiple obstacles to face

For many women, reaching a health facility has become an ordeal. Armed clashes, shifting frontlines, checkpoints, roads blocked by mountains of rubbish, transport costs and forced displacement complicate every consultation.

“Patient transfers are extremely difficult: transport is limited, and functional maternity and neonatal units are scarce,” says Naomi Lubin, an MSF supervising midwife.

Added to this is another challenge: some women are reluctant to leave their neighbourhood for fear of being identified with their place of residence. In a city divided between neighbourhoods controlled by armed groups and others by the authorities, an address can be enough to stigmatise a person or lead others to suspect them of having links to an armed group. Leaving one’s neighbourhood to go to hospital can then become life-threatening.

“My two-year-old child hasn't been vaccinated for a year and a half because I can't leave the area,” says a woman and MSF patient. “I don't want to go out with my identity card with my address indicated. I'm scared. You could get killed.”

Like many other women living in Port-au-Prince, violence is disrupting many aspects of her life, including access to healthcare.

My two-year-old child hasn't been vaccinated for a year and a half because I can't leave the area.

Maintaining healthcare despite the crisis

In response, MSF has set up mobile activities to bring care closer to the communities. Every week, medical teams provide general healthcare in former schools or churches, in multiple neighbourhoods, offering consultations for several hours. In the first half of 2026, they provided 4,500 sexual and reproductive health consultations.

To strengthen the continuity of care in the long term, MSF is also investing in the rehabilitation of the Isaïe Jeanty Maternity hospital in Cité Soleil, an existing public facility.2 Working alongside the Ministry of Public Health and Population, the teams provide emergency obstetric care, including caesarean sections, as well as contraception and care for victims and survivors of sexual violence.

In the first half of 2026, staff assisted with 929 deliveries, including 285 emergency caesarean sections. 257 patients were also referred, with their newborns, to other health facilities for the management of serious complications.

Despite these efforts, people’s needs remain immense. Insecurity continues to limit the movement of patients and medical staff.

“When clashes affect our medical facilities, we have to suspend our activities and evacuate the premises,” Diana Manilla Arroyo, MSF head of mission in Haiti. “This has happened twice in the last two months. These suspensions drastically reduce referral options and complicate the management of obstetric emergencies, as well as many other sexual and reproductive health needs.”

Ensuring continued access to this care remains essential to safeguarding the health and lives of thousands of women and girls in Port-au-Prince.

item.title: Haiti: Do everything possible to protect the population from the effects of escalating armed violence
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Since mid-April 2026, armed clashes have been raging in several areas of Port-au-Prince, Artibonite, the central region and, more recently, in the South-East. The spread of violence is causing the living conditions of already severely affected communities to deteriorate further. Meanwhile, the prospect of new offensive operations is raising fears of increased humanitarian consequences if all necessary precautions are not taken.

"Areas that just yesterday we still considered safe are now becoming unsafe. There is nowhere left for people to take shelter," said Marisela Silva Chau, ICRC Head of Delegation in Haiti.

Growing insecurity is only part of it: the very fabric of people's daily life is unravelling. The mounting consequences of violence, including repeated displacement, limited access to health care and dwindling livelihoods, hit the most vulnerable hardest.

"Each new wave of violence pushes families who already had almost nothing left even further into hardship. Mothers no longer know where they can sleep safely, children are born and raised amid the sound of gunfire, and the wounded sometimes have nowhere to go for medical care," Silva Chau added.

In densely populated areas, offensive operations could lead to an escalation in armed violence in the heart of residential neighbourhoods, new waves of displacement and an already swamped health-care system no longer being able to handle the influx of patients. They could also cause an increase in the number of people imprisoned for violent crimes, overwhelming a prison system that is already at capacity and in which conditions are deteriorating.

"Any scale-up of operations in such densely populated areas must be accompanied by all necessary precautions to spare the civilian population and to prevent a surge in humanitarian needs. Protecting local communities must remain the top priority," said Silva Chau.

In the second half of 2026, internal displacement in the country reached unprecedented levels. According to a new United Nations tally, nearly 1.5 million people have fled their homes, while more than half the population is in need of emergency humanitarian aid.

In light of this situation, the ICRC is continuing its dialogue with all weapon bearers, particularly through awareness-raising sessions on applicable international law and norms. We urge them to conduct their operations in compliance with international law, particularly with regard to the use of force, and underscore the need to effectively protect civilians–including in the planning and conduct of operations and by safeguarding humanitarian action, ensuring safe access to vulnerable populations and protecting detainees.

Our humanitarian response in Haiti from January to June 2026:

Access to health, emergency and trauma services

  • More than 3,691 people with weapon injuries and other patients transported by ICRC-supported emergency services (ambulances and community transport)
  • 380 people with weapon injuries treated at 5 hospitals with ICRC support
  • Approximately 120,000 people served by 3 ICRC-supported health centres in the areas of Port-au-Prince most affected by armed violence
  • Almost 10,000 internally displaced people cared for at 1 ICRC-supported mobile clinic
  • 20-bed emergency department at CHOSCAL hospital renovated

Protecting vulnerable populations and restoring family links

  • More than 100 victims of armed violence (including sexual violence) received emergency care from the ICRC
  • More than 1,200 hygiene kits were supplied to organizations looking after vulnerable people
  • More than 1,000 returnees and internally displaced people received help re-establishing contact with their families, in partnership with the Haitian Red Cross

Improving living conditions for residents and displaced people

  • More than 1,000 woollen blankets distributed at sites for internally displaced people (IDPs)
  • 500 hygiene kits distributed at IDP sites
  • More than 500 solar family lamps distributed to improve lighting and the security of families at IDP sites
  • More than 750 metres of road cleaned, helping to improve the living environment for more than 25,000 people

item.title: Haiti: Haïti : mettre tout en œuvre pour protéger la population face à une violence armée qui s’étend
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Depuis la mi-avril 2026, les affrontements armés embrasent plusieurs zones de Port-au-Prince, de l’Artibonite, de la région du Centre et, plus récemment, du Sud-Est. Face à cette expansion de la violence, des populations fortement éprouvées voient leurs conditions de vie se détériorer, tandis que la perspective de nouvelles opérations offensives fait craindre un alourdissement des conséquences humanitaires si toutes les précautions ne sont pas prises.

« Des zones que nous considérions encore hier comme relativement sûres basculent aujourd'hui dans l'insécurité. La population n'a plus où se réfugier », déclare Marisela Silva Chau, Cheffe de Délégation du CICR en Haïti.

Au-delà de l'insécurité qui gagne du terrain, c'est le quotidien même des habitants qui se délite. Déplacements répétés, accès réduits aux soins, moyens de subsistance épuisés : les conséquences de la violence s'accumulent et pèsent d'abord sur les plus vulnérables.

« Chaque nouvelle vague de violence enfonce un peu plus des familles qui n'avaient déjà presque plus rien. Des mères ne savent plus où dormir en sécurité, des enfants naissent et grandissent au rythme des armes, des blessés n'ont parfois nulle part où se faire soigner », ajoute Marisela Silva Chau.

Dans les zones densément peuplées, les opérations offensives pourraient entraîner une intensification des affrontements armés au cœur des quartiers habités, de nouvelles vagues de déplacement et la saturation d'un système de santé déjà submergé qui pourrait ne plus absorber l'afflux. Elles risqueraient également d'accroître le nombre de personnes détenues en lien avec la violence, submergeant un système pénitentiaire déjà à bout de capacités, où les conditions de détention se dégradent.

« Toute intensification des opérations dans des zones aussi densément peuplées doit s'accompagner de toutes les précautions nécessaires pour que la population soit épargnée et pour éviter une explosion des besoins humanitaires. La protection des populations locales doit rester la priorité absolue », souligne Marisela Silva Chau.

Au deuxième semestre de 2026, le déplacement interne atteint des niveaux sans précédent dans le pays. Selon un nouveau décompte de l'ONU, presque 1,5 million de personnes ont fui leurs foyers, tandis que plus de la moitié de la population a besoin d'une aide humanitaire d'urgence.

Face à cette situation, le CICR poursuit son dialogue avec l'ensemble des porteurs d'armes, notamment à travers des sessions de sensibilisation au droit et aux normes internationales applicables. Il les appelle à conduire leurs opérations dans le respect du droit international, notamment en matière d'usage de la force, et insiste sur la protection effective des populations, y compris dans la planification et la conduite des opérations, la préservation de l'action humanitaire, l'accès sécurisé aux populations vulnérables et la protection des personnes détenues.

Notre réponse humanitaire de janvier à juin 2026 en Haïti :

Accès aux services de santé, d’urgence, et de traumatologie

  • Plus de 3’691 patients et blessés par armes transportés par services d’urgence (ambulances et transporteurs communautaires) soutenus par le CICR.
  • Soutien au fonctionnement de 5 hôpitaux ayant prise en charge 380 blessés par armes
  • 3 centres de santé soutenus couvrant une population d’environ 120’000 personnes vivant dans les zones les plus touchées par la violence armée à Port-au-Prince ;
  • 1 projet de cliniques mobiles soutenu pour près de 10’000 déplacés internes ;
  • Réhabilitation du service des urgences de l’hôpital CHOSCAL d’une capacité de 20 lits.

Protection des populations vulnérables et des liens familiaux

  • Plus de 100 victimes de violence armée (y compris la violence sexuelle) ont reçu une aide d’urgence de la part du CICR.
  • Plus de 1’200 kits d'hygiène fournis à des institutions de prise en charge de personnes vulnérables.
  • Plus de 1’000 retournés au pays et personnes déplacées internes (PDI) assistés, en partenariat avec la Croix-Rouge Haïtienne, pour renouer contact avec leurs proches.

Amélioration des conditions de vie des populations (résidentes et déplacées)

  • Plus de 1’000 couvertures de laine ont été distribuées dans les sites de personnes déplacées internes (PDI).
  • 500 kits d’hygiène distribués dans les sites PDI.
  • Plus de 500 lampes solaires familiales distribuées pour faciliter la luminosité et la sécurité des familles dans les sites PDI.
  • Plus de 750 mètres de routes ont été nettoyés, contribuant à améliorer l’environnement de vie de plus de 25**’**000 bénéficiaires.

item.title: Haiti: Country conditions remain unsafe for returns, new report finds
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants

USCRI has published an updated assessment of humanitarian and security conditions in Haiti, warning that the country remains unsafe for the return of Haitian nationals as the United States moves to terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for more than 330,000 Haitians. The report builds on USCRI's 2024 Haiti country conditions report and draws on interviews with five experts, including three based in Haiti, conducted through July 2026.

Security situation

Armed gangs control an estimated 80–90 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and have expanded their presence, including previously safer southeastern areas. More than one million people are internally displaced and at least 16,000 people have been killed since 2022. The report traces the collapse of state authority to the 2018 fuel-subsidy protests, the indefinite postponement of elections in 2019, President Jovenel Moïse's rule by decree, and his assassination in July 2021, which opened a power vacuum that gangs moved to fill. Citing a 2021 Harvard Law School/RNDDH investigation, the report describes gang attacks on civilians as systematic rather than random, alleging coordination between gang leaders and government officials to suppress political opposition, with perpetrators of documented massacres remaining unprosecuted.

Humanitarian needs

An estimated 6.4 million people need urgent humanitarian assistance. The most recent IPC analysis (March–June 2026) found 5.83 million people, more than half the population, facing acute food insecurity, including 1.2 million children under five. A 2023–2024 IPC malnutrition assessment found 125,000 children severely malnourished. Only 10 percent of the country's in-patient medical facilities remain operational; 70 percent of healthcare facilities in Port-au-Prince were closed as of 2025. The report also documents a resurgence of diphtheria (159 cases reported as of June 2026, more than the rest of the Americas combined) and an outbreak of a scabies-like skin disease in displacement camps, where residents lack access to clean water and sanitation.

Sexual and gender-based violence

The UN recorded a 163 percent increase in verified sexual violence cases in 2025, which the report notes likely understates the true scale given severe underreporting. UNICEF has reported a 1,000 percent increase in sexual violence against minors since 2023. Data from an MSF clinic in Port-au-Prince recorded nearly 17,000 survivors treated between 2015 and 2025, 57 percent of whom were attacked by members of armed groups.

Deportation and return risk

The report argues returns to Haiti carry both practical and protection risks. The FAA has extended its ban on U.S. commercial flights landing in Port-au-Prince following gang attacks on aircraft. Displaced people returning often have no home to go back to, and navigating gang checkpoints from the airport can be life-threatening. Interviewees told USCRI that returnees — particularly those associated with the diaspora, government, or civil society — are frequently viewed by gangs as threats and targeted for kidnapping or violence. Groupe d'Appui aux Rapatriés et Réfugiés reported more than 68,000 Haitians were deported to Haiti in the first three months of 2026 alone, up from 55,000 in the same period of 2025, with deportations from the United States expected to rise.

The report concludes that returning individuals to conditions of well-founded persecution risk would violate the principle of non-refoulement, a binding U.S. obligation, and calls for documented country conditions, rather than a general narrative of "fixed" crisis, to inform policy on Haitians' protection status.

Full report: https://refugees.org/haiti-is-not-safe-country-conditions-2026/
